name: Excellent Arrays
description: Let's call an integer array $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ good if $$$a_i \neq i$$$ for each $$$i$$$. Let $$$F(a)$$$ be the number of pairs $$$(i, j)$$$ ($$$1 \le i \lt j \le n$$$) such that $$$a_i + a_j = i + j$$$. Let's say that an array $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ is excellent if: $$$a$$$ is good ; $$$l \le a_i \le r$$$ for each $$$i$$$; $$$F(a)$$$ is the maximum possible among all good arrays of size $$$n$$$. Given $$$n$$$, $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$, calculate the number of excellent arrays modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 1000$$$) — the number of test cases. The first and only line of each test case contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$l$$$, and $$$r$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$; $$$-10^9 \le l \le 1$$$; $$$n \le r \le 10^9$$$). It's guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ doesn't exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print the number of excellent arrays modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
approach_summary: Exploit monotonicity of two-pointer invariant [L, R]. Advance R while shifting L forward to maintain validity, running in O(N) amortized time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1550D — Excellent Arrays [34. Two Pointers]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: When scanning contiguous subarrays or paired indices, advancing the right pointer $R$ monotonically tightens or relaxes the constraint, allowing the left pointer $L$ to only advance forward without ever needing to reset backwards.
